questionText:
Let $G$ be a simple, finite, undirected graph with vertex set \{v_1, \dots, v_n\}. Let $\Delta(G)$ denote the maximum degree of $G$ and let $\mathbb{N} = \{1, 2, \dots\}$ denote the set of all possible colors. Color the vertices of $G$ using the following greedy strategy:
for $i = 1, \dots, n$
$$\text{color}(v_i) \leftarrow \min\{j \in \mathbb{N} : \text{ no neighbour of } v_i \text{ is colored } j\}$$

Which of the following statements is/are TRUE?
options: This procedure results in a proper vertex coloring of $G$.
The number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G) + 1$.
The number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G)$.
The number of colors used is equal to the chromatic number of $G$.
explanation:
Step 1: Proper Vertex Coloring (Option A)
The greedy algorithm assigns to each vertex $v_i$ the smallest color in $\mathbb{N}$ that is not already assigned to any of its neighbors. Since no adjacent vertices share the same color, this process always results in a valid (proper) vertex coloring of $G$. Thus, Statement (A) is TRUE.

Step 2: Number of Colors Used (Options B & C)
When coloring vertex $v_i$, it has at most $\text{deg}(v_i) \le \Delta(G)$ neighbors. Consequently, at most $\Delta(G)$ colors are unavailable for $v_i$. Even if all neighbors of $v_i$ are assigned distinct colors from $\{1, 2, \dots, \Delta(G)\}$, the color $\Delta(G) + 1$ is always available. Hence, the total number of colors used is at most $\Delta(G) + 1$. Therefore, Statement (B) is TRUE.
Statement (C) is FALSE because complete graphs $K_n$ require $n = \Delta(G) + 1$ colors.

Step 3: Chromatic Number (Option D)
The output of the greedy coloring algorithm depends heavily on the ordering of vertices and does not always yield the minimum number of colors needed to color $G$ (the chromatic number $\chi(G)$). For instance, with an unfavorable vertex ordering, a bipartite graph (which has $\chi(G) = 2$) can require significantly more colors. Thus, Statement (D) is FALSE.

Conclusion:
The correct statements are A and B.
